questions.stem: A 45-year-old man and his wife come to the emergency department in January with headache, nausea and dizziness that started this morning. After a power outage 2 days ago, they have run a gasoline generator in their closed garage. He is alert but at times confused. Respirations are 18/min. Pulse oximetry shows 99% on room air. Arterial blood gas with co-oximetry shows: PaO2 98 mm Hg, hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, carboxyhemoglobin 26% (normal less than 3%), and methemoglobin 1%. Which mechanism best explains his tissue hypoxia?
choices: Less oxygen dissolved in the plasma
Oxidation of heme iron to the ferric (Fe3+) state
A right-shifted curve that slows O2 loading in the lungs
Fewer O2 sites on hemoglobin and a left-shifted curve
Thickened alveolar walls that limit O2 diffusion
questions.explanation: **CO** binds hemoglobin much more tightly than O2, so fewer heme sites carry O2 and **O2 content falls**. CO on one heme also makes the other hemes hold O2 more tightly (**left shift**), so less O2 is released in the tissues. The PaO2 is normal because dissolved O2 is not affected, and standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin. Methemoglobinemia (Fe3+) is tempting because it also lowers content with a normal PaO2, but his methemoglobin is normal, and significant methemoglobinemia gives an SpO2 near 85%.
questions.explanation_pt: O **CO** liga-se à hemoglobina com muito mais força que o O2, então menos grupos heme transportam O2 e o **conteúdo de O2 cai**. O CO em um heme também faz os outros hemes segurarem o O2 com mais força (**desvio para a esquerda**), e menos O2 é liberado nos tecidos. A PaO2 é normal porque o O2 dissolvido não é afetado, e a oximetria de pulso convencional lê a carboxi-hemoglobina como oxi-hemoglobina. A metemoglobinemia (Fe3+) é tentadora porque também reduz o conteúdo com PaO2 normal, mas a metemoglobina dele é normal, e a metemoglobinemia significativa dá SpO2 próxima de 85%.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and 3 months of fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion. At sea level on room air, her results are: hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, SaO2 98%, and PaO2 95 mm Hg. Her cardiac output is normal. Her physician uses the arterial O2 content equation to compare possible changes. Which change would raise her arterial O2 content the most?
choices: Raising hemoglobin from 6 to 9 g/dL
Raising PaO2 from 95 to 500 mm Hg with 100% oxygen
Raising SaO2 from 98% to 100%
Raising cardiac output by 50%
Shifting the curve to the right with more 2,3-BPG
questions.explanation: O2 content = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2. Now it is about 1.34 × 6 × 0.98 + 0.003 × 95 ≈ 7.9 + 0.3 ≈ **8.2 mL O2/dL**; with Hb 9 it is about 11.8 + 0.3 ≈ **12.1 mL/dL** (a rise of about 3.9). With 100% O2 (PaO2 500, SaO2 100%) it is only about 8.0 + 1.5 ≈ 9.5 mL/dL, because dissolved O2 adds little and her Hb is already almost fully saturated. Raising cardiac output is tempting, but it raises O2 **delivery**, not the O2 content of each deciliter of blood.
questions.explanation_pt: Conteúdo de O2 = 1,34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0,003 × PaO2. Agora é cerca de 1,34 × 6 × 0,98 + 0,003 × 95 ≈ 7,9 + 0,3 ≈ **8,2 mL O2/dL**; com Hb 9 fica cerca de 11,8 + 0,3 ≈ **12,1 mL/dL** (aumento de cerca de 3,9). Com O2 a 100% (PaO2 500, SaO2 100%) fica só cerca de 8,0 + 1,5 ≈ 9,5 mL/dL, porque o O2 dissolvido acrescenta pouco e a Hb dela já está quase totalmente saturada. Aumentar o débito cardíaco é tentador, mas isso aumenta a **oferta** de O2, não o conteúdo de O2 de cada decilitro de sangue.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has shortness of breath when he walks. At rest on room air, his pulse oximetry is 94%. During a 6-minute walk test, it falls to 84%, his heart rate rises from 80/min to 118/min, and his respiratory rate rises from 18/min to 30/min. Which mechanism best explains the fall in oxygen saturation during exercise?
choices: Opening of a right-to-left shunt through the foramen ovale
Alveolar hypoventilation from respiratory muscle fatigue
Higher O2 affinity of hemoglobin in the lung capillaries
Collapse of small airways during fast expiration
Short transit time for O2 across a thickened membrane
questions.explanation: In a healthy lung, O2 reaches equilibrium early in the capillary, so there is time to spare. In **fibrosis**, the thick membrane slows O2 transfer; during exercise the higher cardiac output **shortens capillary transit time**, and blood leaves before it is fully loaded (**diffusion limitation**). Hypoventilation is tempting because he is tired, but his breathing rate rises sharply, and patients with fibrosis usually breathe fast with a low or normal PaCO2. Small airway collapse is a feature of obstructive disease, not fibrosis.
questions.explanation_pt: No pulmão saudável, o O2 entra em equilíbrio no início do capilar, então sobra tempo. Na **fibrose**, a membrana espessa retarda a passagem do O2; no exercício, o débito cardíaco maior **encurta o tempo de trânsito capilar**, e o sangue sai antes de estar totalmente carregado (**limitação da difusão**). A hipoventilação é tentadora porque ele está cansado, mas a frequência respiratória dele sobe muito, e pacientes com fibrose costumam respirar rápido, com PaCO2 baixa ou normal. O colapso de pequenas vias aéreas é próprio da doença obstrutiva, não da fibrose.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has 1 week of coughing up blood and 3 days of dark urine. He does not smoke. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL and serum creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows red cell casts. Pulmonary function tests show an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.82, TLC 98% of predicted, and DLCO 138% of predicted. Which best explains his DLCO result?
choices: A larger red cell mass in the lung capillaries
Hemoglobin in alveolar blood that takes up inhaled CO
Antibody-related thickening of the alveolar basement membrane
Loss of alveolar walls and capillary surface area
Air trapping that holds the test gas in the lungs
questions.explanation: Hemoptysis with glomerulonephritis suggests a **pulmonary-renal syndrome** such as anti-GBM disease, with **alveolar hemorrhage**. Red cells in the alveoli bind the inhaled CO, so more CO leaves the test gas and **DLCO rises** even though he is anemic. Basement membrane injury is tempting if you suspect anti-GBM disease, but a thicker barrier would lower the DLCO, not raise it. A larger red cell mass (polycythemia) also raises DLCO, but his hemoglobin is low.
questions.explanation_pt: Hemoptise com glomerulonefrite sugere uma **síndrome pulmão-rim**, como a doença anti-MBG, com **hemorragia alveolar**. As hemácias nos alvéolos ligam o CO inalado, então mais CO sai do gás do teste e a **DLCO aumenta**, mesmo com anemia. A lesão da membrana basal é tentadora se você suspeita de doença anti-MBG, mas uma barreira mais espessa reduziria a DLCO, não a aumentaria. Uma massa eritrocitária maior (policitemia) também aumenta a DLCO, mas a hemoglobina dele está baixa.

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old man runs on a treadmill. Consider the blood that flows through the capillaries of his working leg muscles. CO2 moves from the muscle cells into the plasma and then into the red blood cells. Which event occurs in the red blood cells in this capillary bed?
choices: Hemoglobin binds O2 more tightly as CO2 rises
Bicarbonate enters the cell in exchange for chloride
Bicarbonate leaves the cell in exchange for chloride
Carbonic anhydrase turns bicarbonate back into CO2
Oxyhemoglobin takes up most of the H+ that forms
questions.explanation: In the tissues, red cell **carbonic anhydrase** turns CO2 and water into H+ and **HCO3-**. HCO3- leaves the cell through the band 3 anion exchanger while Cl- enters (**chloride shift**), so most CO2 travels as plasma bicarbonate. The H+ is buffered by **deoxyhemoglobin**, which binds H+ better than oxyhemoglobin (Haldane effect). The reverse exchange (HCO3- entering for Cl-) is tempting, but it happens in the lungs, where carbonic anhydrase turns bicarbonate back into CO2 to be breathed out.
questions.explanation_pt: Nos tecidos, a **anidrase carbônica** da hemácia transforma CO2 e água em H+ e **HCO3-**. O HCO3- sai da célula pelo trocador aniônico banda 3 enquanto o Cl- entra (**desvio do cloreto**), então a maior parte do CO2 viaja como bicarbonato no plasma. O H+ é tamponado pela **desoxi-hemoglobina**, que liga H+ melhor que a oxi-hemoglobina (efeito Haldane). A troca inversa (HCO3- entrando no lugar do Cl-) é tentadora, mas ocorre nos pulmões, onde a anidrase carbônica transforma o bicarbonato de volta em CO2 para ser expirado.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with severe COPD comes to the emergency department with a COPD exacerbation. On room air, arterial blood gas shows pH 7.35, PaCO2 54 mm Hg, PaO2 46 mm Hg, and HCO3- 29 mEq/L. He is given high-concentration oxygen through a non-rebreather mask. One hour later he is drowsy. His respiratory rate (22/min) and minute ventilation are the same as on arrival. Repeat arterial blood gas shows pH 7.25, PaCO2 70 mm Hg, PaO2 140 mm Hg, and HCO3- 30 mEq/L. Which mechanism most likely explains the rise in PaCO2?
choices: Loss of the hypoxic drive to breathe
More CO2 production from a higher metabolic rate
A left shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve
Slower diffusion of CO2 across the alveolar membrane
Release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: In COPD, **hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction** sends blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli. High inspired O2 relaxes these vessels, so more blood flows to low-V/Q units and less to well-ventilated ones (**more effective dead space**); the **Haldane effect** (oxygenated Hb releases CO2) adds to the rise. Loss of hypoxic drive is the classic tempting answer, but his minute ventilation did not fall. CO2 diffuses about 20 times more easily than O2, so diffusion does not limit CO2 removal.
questions.explanation_pt: Na DPOC, a **vasoconstrição pulmonar hipóxica** desvia o sangue dos alvéolos mal ventilados. O O2 em alta concentração relaxa esses vasos, então mais sangue vai para unidades com V/Q baixa e menos para as bem ventiladas (**mais espaço morto efetivo**); o **efeito Haldane** (a Hb oxigenada libera CO2) soma-se ao aumento. A perda do estímulo hipóxico é a resposta clássica tentadora, mas a ventilação-minuto dele não caiu. O CO2 difunde cerca de 20 vezes mais facilmente que o O2, então a difusão não limita a eliminação de CO2.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after a car crash, with heavy bleeding from a pelvic fracture. Over 2 hours he receives many units of packed red blood cells that had been stored for several weeks. Compared with his own red cells, how do the transfused cells most likely behave during the first hours after transfusion?
choices: Higher O2 affinity because of low 2,3-BPG
Lower O2 affinity because of high 2,3-BPG
Higher O2 affinity because of more fetal hemoglobin
Lower O2 affinity because of ferric heme iron
Normal O2 affinity with less hemoglobin per cell
questions.explanation: During storage, red cell glycolysis slows and **2,3-BPG** levels fall. Less 2,3-BPG means **higher O2 affinity** and a **left-shifted curve**, so the transfused cells load O2 well in the lungs but release less in the tissues. Levels recover over the next few days. The reverse choice (high 2,3-BPG) is tempting because 2,3-BPG rises in chronic hypoxia and anemia, but that is a response of the patient's own living red cells, not of stored cells.
questions.explanation_pt: Durante o armazenamento, a glicólise da hemácia diminui e os níveis de **2,3-BPG** caem. Menos 2,3-BPG significa **maior afinidade pelo O2** e **curva desviada para a esquerda**, então as hemácias transfundidas captam bem o O2 nos pulmões, mas liberam menos nos tecidos. Os níveis se recuperam nos dias seguintes. A alternativa inversa (2,3-BPG alto) é tentadora porque o 2,3-BPG aumenta na hipóxia crônica e na anemia, mas essa é uma resposta das hemácias vivas do próprio paciente, não das hemácias armazenadas.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman climbs quickly to a mountain camp where the barometric pressure is 380 mm Hg. She has a mild headache, but no cough, and her lungs are clear on auscultation. On room air (FiO2 0.21), arterial blood gas shows PaCO2 24 mm Hg and PaO2 36 mm Hg. Assume a water vapor pressure of 47 mm Hg and a respiratory quotient of 0.8. Which best explains her hypoxemia?
choices: Alveolar hypoventilation
Fluid in the alveoli that limits O2 diffusion
Right-to-left shunt within the lungs
Low partial pressure of inspired oxygen
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
questions.explanation: Inspired PO2 = 0.21 × (380 − 47) ≈ 70 mm Hg, so PAO2 ≈ 70 − 24/0.8 = 70 − 30 ≈ **40 mm Hg**. The **A-a gradient** is about 40 − 36 = 4 mm Hg, which is normal, and her PaCO2 is low, so the cause is a **low inspired PO2**, not lung disease or hypoventilation. High-altitude pulmonary edema is tempting at this height, but fluid in the alveoli would widen the gradient, and her lungs are clear.
questions.explanation_pt: PO2 inspirada = 0,21 × (380 − 47) ≈ 70 mm Hg, então PAO2 ≈ 70 − 24/0,8 = 70 − 30 ≈ **40 mm Hg**. O **gradiente A-a** é cerca de 40 − 36 = 4 mm Hg, ou seja, normal, e a PaCO2 dela está baixa, então a causa é a **PO2 inspirada baixa**, não doença pulmonar nem hipoventilação. O edema pulmonar de grande altitude é tentador nessa altura, mas líquido nos alvéolos aumentaria o gradiente, e os pulmões dela estão limpos.
